compile

kum-PYL -- built from 'com-' (together) plus a root related to gathering or heaping. · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To compile is to collect information from different sources and arrange it in a single, organized form.

Before the trial, lawyers had to compile thousands of pages of evidence into a single binder.

Example

A librarian gathers hundreds of scattered newspaper clippings, letters, and photographs from an entire century and organizes them into one carefully indexed digital archive.

That careful gathering and organizing of scattered pieces into one complete whole is exactly what compile means. Unlike 'scatter,' which spreads things apart, compile brings them together.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

collect: To collect is simply to bring together items from different places -- coins, samples, permission slips. To compile goes a step further: after the pieces are collected, you arrange them into one organized, finished form, like a report or a handbook. Collecting is step one; compiling includes the organizing.

amass: To amass is to pile up a large quantity of something over time -- a fortune, an army, a mountain of evidence. Amassing cares about how much you end up with; to compile cares about arrangement, pulling scattered information into one organized form whatever its size.

collate: To collate is to check and arrange pages or copies that already exist into their proper order. To compile starts earlier and does more: you first hunt down information from different sources, then organize it into a single finished form. Collating only orders; compiling gathers and builds.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

scatter: to separate and spread widely in different directions

disperse: to spread over a wide area

Where it sits · how much structure the collecting adds — gather → compile → assemble

gather vs. compile: Gather is a more everyday, general word than compile -- gather can describe collecting almost anything, while compile specifically implies organizing collected information into a finished, structured form.

assemble vs. compile: Assemble can feel more deliberate than compile in some contexts: compile often focuses on gathering information or data, while assemble can suggest carefully fitting separate pieces together into a complete structure.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — com-

prefix — com-: together (Latin)

root — -pile

root — -pile: to heap, pack together (Latin (compilare))

Put it together

Put it together: Latin compilare meant 'to plunder' or 'heap together,' built from com- ('together') and pilare, related to piling things up. To compile something, at its root, is to heap scattered pieces together into one organized pile -- the same root that gives us compilation.

Use the root in a new word: compilation

Use the root in a new word: compilation: The band released a compilation of their greatest hits from the past two decades.
